newsitem.title: CANADA: CBRS reaffirms Ontario ratings at AA and A-1+.
newsitem.headline: CBRS reaffirms Ontario ratings at AA and A-1+.

text.p: Canadian Bond Rating Service said on Friday it reaffirmed the province of Ontario's long and short-term ratings at AA and A-1+, respectively, with a stable outlook.

CBRS said that with Ontario's recent changes to education, social services and municipalities, the province moved to limit its exposure to many items that could have affected its financial position in periods of low economic growth.
Ontario's restructuring was viewed favorably because the provincial government would share costs for some potentially expensive programs with municipalities, CBRS said.
On January 1, 1998, funding for school boards in the province will become a provincial responsibility and school board taxes will be removed from residential property tax bills.

CBRS said the province was also restructuring its education system to reduce the number of school boards and school trustees and replace Ontario's five-year secondary school program with a four-year program.

The bond rating service said that education funding might continue to increase due to student growth, but fewer boards, reduced capital expenditure and a shorter program should result in lower financial commitments and grants being required from the province.
CBRS said Ontario's balanced budget timetable was not affected by the changes, and the provincial income tax rate would continue to decline.
The general welfare assistance (GWA) funding will be altered next year, changing the funding to a 50/50 share in funding from an 80/20 province-to-municipality ratio.
Most municipalities, except those in remote areas, will become responsible for fully funding a host of programs.

CBRS said a number of issues were unresolved and the resulting financial impact on many participants was yet to be determined. For example, if downloading occurred without adjusting for the various levels of services currently provided, some regions could end up assuming greater costs than others.
CBRS said it remained to be seen whether the municipal tax base could maintain increasing levels of health services at their current levels.

"Furthermore, the changes provided by the province do not, in our opinion, provide municipalities with a greater ability to collect revenues from alternate sources," CBRS said. "In (our) opinion, most of these programs will end up being funded through higher property taxes."

CBRS said it would re-evaluate the province's position when Ontario presented its 1997 budget and would also assess the impact of the changes on other participants on a case by case basis since it appeared the Greater Toronto Area would be affected significantly.
